title: Asthma & COPD: Airflow Limitation, Exacerbation Rescue and Inhaler Self-Management
html:
Asthma and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) can both cause wheeze, cough, dyspnea, and airflow limitation, but their patterns and long-term treatment are not interchangeable. During an exacerbation, the RN prioritizes work of breathing, gas exchange, mentation, fatigue, and response to treatment—not the loudness of wheezing alone. Long-term safety depends on anti-inflammatory or bronchodilator therapy matched to diagnosis, reliable inhaler technique, risk reduction, and a written action plan.

Learning goals

  • Differentiate variable asthma from persistent COPD airflow limitation using history and objective testing.
  • Recognize impending respiratory failure even when wheezing decreases.
  • Prioritize oxygen, bronchodilator, corticosteroid, ventilation, and reassessment during acute exacerbations.
  • Explain why asthma requires inhaled corticosteroid-containing treatment and why COPD regimens are individualized.
  • Teach correct metered-dose, dry-powder, soft-mist, spacer, and nebulizer technique.
  • Plan smoking cessation, vaccination, trigger control, pulmonary rehabilitation, and follow-up.

Start with breathing, speech, and mental status

Observe position, ability to speak, respiratory rate and pattern, accessory-muscle use, retractions, chest movement, audible sounds, cough, sputum, color, alertness, agitation, and fatigue before completing a detailed history. Measure oxygen saturation in context, auscultate air movement throughout both lungs, and trend pulse and blood pressure.

Severe distress, inability to speak more than words, exhaustion, drowsiness, confusion, cyanosis, a silent or nearly silent chest, poor respiratory effort, hypotension, or worsening gas exchange signals life-threatening obstruction or respiratory failure. A quieter chest after previously loud wheezing can mean less airflow—not improvement.

Less wheeze can mean less air
Judge improvement by easier breathing, better speech, stronger air entry, improving oxygenation and ventilation, lower distress, and objective airflow—not sound alone.

Asthma is variable airway inflammation

Asthma involves chronic airway inflammation, variable bronchoconstriction, mucus, and airway hyperresponsiveness. Symptoms often vary over time and intensity and may be triggered by viral infection, allergens, exercise, smoke, occupational exposure, weather, or medications. Nighttime or early-morning symptoms and episodic reversibility support the pattern.

Diagnosis combines a characteristic history with evidence of variable expiratory airflow limitation, often using spirometry before and after bronchodilator, peak-flow variability, or other testing. A normal examination between episodes does not exclude asthma. Alternative or coexisting causes of dyspnea and cough must still be considered.

COPD is persistent and heterogeneous

COPD is persistent airflow obstruction caused by airway and/or alveolar abnormalities, commonly related to tobacco smoke but also occupational or environmental exposures, abnormal lung development, recurrent injury, or alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency. Chronic bronchitis describes chronic productive cough; emphysema describes destruction of alveolar walls and loss of elastic recoil. Many clients have overlapping features.

Consider COPD with chronic dyspnea, cough or sputum, recurrent lower-respiratory infections, activity limitation, and relevant exposure. Post-bronchodilator spirometry is required to confirm persistent obstruction. Severity and treatment are not based on FEV1 alone; symptoms, exacerbation history, oxygenation, comorbidities, function, and client goals matter.

Assess the exacerbation and its trigger

Clarify baseline symptoms, usual oxygen, prior intubation or ICU care, rescue-inhaler use, controller adherence and access, recent peak flow when used, sick contacts, fever, sputum change, allergens, smoke, aspiration, sedatives, and cardiac symptoms. Review inhaler devices and ask the client to demonstrate technique.

Possible triggers or mimics include viral or bacterial infection, pneumonia, pneumothorax, pulmonary embolism, heart failure, acute coronary syndrome, dysrhythmia, anaphylaxis, upper-airway obstruction, medication interruption, and environmental exposure. New unilateral absent breath sounds, pleuritic pain, hypotension, focal findings, edema, or fever should widen the differential.

Oxygen is titrated—never reflexively withheld

Give supplemental oxygen promptly for hypoxemia and titrate to the prescribed target while assessing ventilation. In severe asthma, correct hypoxemia and prepare ventilatory support if fatigue or rising carbon dioxide develops. In COPD, some clients are vulnerable to worsening hypercapnia with excessive oxygen, but this is not a reason to leave a hypoxemic client untreated. Use a controlled device, an individualized target, clinical reassessment, and blood-gas data when indicated.

Pulse oximetry estimates oxygen saturation but does not measure carbon dioxide or ventilation. A client can have an acceptable saturation and still retain carbon dioxide or tire. Trend mentation, respiratory effort, rate, tidal movement, and blood gases when the clinical picture is severe or changing.

Asthma exacerbation: reverse spasm and inflammation

Position upright, minimize exertion, provide oxygen as indicated, and give repeated inhaled rapid bronchodilator therapy under the acute pathway. An inhaled short-acting antimuscarinic is commonly added for severe exacerbations. Systemic corticosteroids should be given early when indicated because they treat inflammation but do not produce immediate bronchodilation.

Monitor symptoms, speech, air entry, respiratory effort, pulse, oxygenation, peak expiratory flow or spirometry when feasible, and adverse effects such as tremor, tachycardia, potassium shift, or hyperglycemia. IV magnesium may be considered in selected severe asthma that responds poorly to initial treatment. Antibiotics are not routine unless bacterial infection is supported.

Prepare early for airway expertise when the client is tiring, confused, drowsy, developing a silent chest, worsening despite therapy, or showing rising carbon dioxide with acidosis. Intubation in severe asthma is high risk because air trapping and dynamic hyperinflation can cause hypotension and barotrauma; experienced support is essential.

COPD exacerbation: support ventilation and treat the cause

A COPD exacerbation is an acute worsening of dyspnea, cough, and/or sputum beyond usual variation. Give controlled oxygen, short-acting bronchodilators, systemic corticosteroid therapy when indicated, and antibiotics when the clinical pattern suggests bacterial infection or ventilatory support is required. Evaluate for pneumonia, heart failure, PE, pneumothorax, or ACS.

Noninvasive positive-pressure ventilation can reduce work of breathing and improve ventilation in selected clients with acute hypercapnic respiratory failure who can protect the airway, cooperate, and manage secretions. Monitor mask fit, skin, synchrony, comfort, mental status, aspiration risk, secretions, gas exchange, and hemodynamics. Worsening acidosis, declining consciousness, inability to protect the airway, severe instability, or failure to improve requires rapid escalation for invasive ventilation.

Air trapping changes bedside care

Obstructed exhalation can cause dynamic hyperinflation, especially when respiratory rate is high. Clients may use pursed-lip breathing to prolong exhalation and reduce airway collapse. Coach a slow breath in and a longer controlled breath out; do not force rapid deep breaths. Space activities, cluster care thoughtfully, and allow recovery time.

Severe air trapping can raise intrathoracic pressure, reduce venous return, and cause hypotension. During mechanical ventilation, longer expiratory time and careful settings are required by the respiratory and critical-care team. Sudden deterioration also requires evaluation for pneumothorax.

Asthma control requires anti-inflammatory treatment

Current asthma strategy recommends inhaled corticosteroid-containing treatment rather than short-acting beta agonist alone for adults and adolescents. A rapid bronchodilator may relieve symptoms, but it does not treat airway inflammation. Depending on the individualized plan, an inhaled corticosteroid-formoterol combination may serve as reliever and controller, or a separate reliever may accompany daily controller therapy.

Frequent reliever use, nighttime symptoms, activity limitation, exacerbations, repeated systemic steroids, or falling lung function indicate poor control or future risk. Before escalating therapy, verify diagnosis, inhaler technique, adherence and affordability, exposure, and comorbidities. Severe asthma may require phenotype assessment and biologic therapy.

COPD maintenance follows symptoms and exacerbations

Long-acting bronchodilators are central to stable COPD treatment. A long-acting beta agonist, long-acting muscarinic antagonist, or combination is selected based on symptoms and exacerbation risk. Inhaled corticosteroids are added for selected clients, particularly when exacerbation history and eosinophilic inflammation support benefit or asthma coexists.

Inhaled corticosteroids in COPD can increase pneumonia risk in susceptible clients and should not be added automatically for dyspnea alone. Evaluate technique, adherence, comorbidities, rehabilitation, and alternate causes before escalation. Do not abruptly remove an effective regimen without clinical review.

Inhaler technique is a clinical skill

Identify the exact device; instructions differ. For a pressurized metered-dose inhaler, shake when required, exhale away from the device, seal lips, begin a slow deep inhalation as the dose is actuated, continue inhaling, hold as able, and wait the directed interval between puffs. A spacer reduces coordination demands and oropharyngeal deposition.

A dry-powder inhaler usually requires a quick, deep inhalation and should not be shaken or exhaled into because moisture can affect the powder. Soft-mist inhalers and breath-actuated devices have their own loading and inhalation steps. Nebulizers require the correct medication, assembly, position, flow source, cleaning, and infection-control plan.

When multiple inhaled drugs are prescribed, follow the written sequence; bronchodilation before an inhaled corticosteroid can improve delivery in some plans. Rinse and spit after inhaled corticosteroids to reduce local candidiasis and dysphonia. Use return demonstration at each transition rather than asking only, “Do you know how?”

Peak flow supports action plans, not diagnosis alone

For selected clients with asthma, peak expiratory flow can show change from a personal best and guide a written green-yellow-red action plan. Use the same meter and technique, stand or sit consistently, reset the indicator, seal lips, blow hard and fast, and record the best of repeated attempts as instructed. Effort and technique affect results.

A peak-flow value does not override severe symptoms. A client who is exhausted, cyanotic, confused, or unable to speak needs emergency care even if a single measurement appears reassuring.

Long-term oxygen and safety

Long-term oxygen therapy benefits selected clients with documented severe chronic resting hypoxemia after appropriate evaluation. Oxygen is prescribed by device, flow or target, and activity/sleep conditions; it is not adjusted casually. Keep oxygen away from smoking, vaping, flames, sparks, oils, and heat sources; secure cylinders and maintain equipment as directed.

Smoking while using oxygen can cause fatal burns and fire. Approach cessation without shame, assess readiness, offer medication and behavioral support, and create a household fire-safety plan.

Prevent future exacerbations

Address tobacco and vaping exposure, occupational triggers, allergens relevant to the individual, medication access, inhaler technique, vaccination, hand hygiene, nutrition, sleep, anxiety, and comorbid heart disease, reflux, obesity, or sleep apnea. Pulmonary rehabilitation improves exercise capacity, symptoms, and quality of life for appropriate COPD clients.

Provide a written action plan that names daily medicines, reliever steps, individualized oxygen instructions, symptom or peak-flow thresholds, who to contact, and when to call emergency services. Arrange follow-up after an exacerbation and reconcile every inhaler because similar devices may contain different drugs.

Apply clinical judgment

  1. Recognize cues: Assess speech, mentation, work of breathing, air entry, respiratory rate, oxygenation, baseline function, cough and sputum, triggers, medications, device technique, prior severe episodes, and comorbidities.
  2. Analyze cues: Distinguish asthma variability from persistent COPD, mild distress from fatigue and failure, hypoxemia from ventilation failure, and exacerbation from pneumonia, PE, pneumothorax, or heart failure.
  3. Prioritize hypotheses: Silent chest, exhaustion, altered mentation, severe hypoxemia, hypercapnic acidosis, pneumothorax, anaphylaxis, and failed noninvasive ventilation require immediate action.
  4. Generate solutions: Position, titrate oxygen, give rapid bronchodilation and anti-inflammatory therapy, treat the trigger, conserve energy, and prepare ventilation support.
  5. Take action: Use the ordered pathway and correct device, monitor continuously when severe, obtain blood gases when indicated, and escalate early rather than waiting for arrest.
  6. Evaluate outcomes: Reassess speech, effort, air entry, oxygenation, ventilation, mentation, peak flow when appropriate, hemodynamics, adverse effects, and teach-back.

Clinical example

A client with asthma initially has loud wheezing but then becomes drowsy, speaks only one word at a time, and has minimal air movement despite repeated bronchodilator treatment. The RN recognizes that the quieter chest reflects worsening obstruction and fatigue, not recovery. Emergency airway support is activated, oxygen and continuous monitoring continue, systemic anti-inflammatory therapy and other protocol-directed rescue measures are prepared, and the team plans controlled ventilation while reassessing mentation, effort, air entry, gas exchange, pulse, and blood pressure.

Asthma and COPD diagnosis, inhaler selection, oxygen targets, bronchodilator and corticosteroid dosing, antibiotic decisions, noninvasive or invasive ventilation, and emergency treatment require current clinical data, authorized orders, local protocols, respiratory expertise, and qualified supervision.
